newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing merger clears final EU hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Boeing merger clears final EU hurdle.

text.p: The European Commission, formally ending a five-month antitrust probe which brought Europe and the United States to the brink of a trade war, cleared on Wednesday a merger between aerospace giants Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.

The decision by the European Union executive, the 15-nation bloc's competition watchdog, was regarded as a formality after Boeing a week ago agreed to last-minute concessions which addressed EU concerns about the merger's impact on the civil aviation market.
EU national competition experts gave their blessing on Friday to the $15 billion deal which will form the world's largest aerospace company, expected to generate $49 billion in revenue this year.
"There was no vote. There was no discussion," an EU source said, referring to the meeting of the 20 European commissioners.
In a statement, the Commission said declared the merger compatible with the EU's common market, subject to Boeing's full compliance with the commitments it had made.

It made clear it would not tolerate any deviation from the agreed terms. "The EU merger regulation allows for appropriate measures to be taken by the Commission in the event of non-compliance by Boeing."

To win EU approval, the Seattle-based aerospace giant pledged not to enforce exclusivity provisions in controversial long-term supply contracts with AMR Corp's American Airlines, Continental Airlines and Delta Air Lines.

It also agreed not to strike any new supply contracts with airlines before August 1, 2007, to keep McDonnell Douglas' commercial aircraft unit in a separate entity for 10 years and to license patents to other aircraft makers.

"These commitments are considered adequate to resolve the identified competition problems," the Commission said. It had earlier threatened to block the merger, saying it would strengthen Boeing's already dominant market position.

EU Research Commissioner Edith Cresson last week said she disagreed with the preliminary EU approval, arguing that the concessions would not prevent Boeing from gaining a near or total monopoly in some markets.

On the other hand, EU Economic Affairs Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy said approval of the merger would be a good thing as it would pave the way for European consortium Airbus to do more US business.

"What would we Europeans have said, we French in particular, if U.S. authorities had imposed conditions or blocked a merger of a French company with a German company. We would have said, 'What business is it of yours?'" he said on Wednesday.
As a result of the merger, Boeing's share of the commercial jet market will increase to 70 percent from its current level of 64 percent, leaving only Airbus in a position to compete.

The Commission said European airlines were expected to account for almost a third of demand for commercial jet aircraft over the next ten years, and that two U.S. firms together had two thirds of the EU market.

The merger, which was announced in December and approved by the two companies' shareholders last Friday, also allows Boeing to reduce its dependence on the commercial aviation sector, as McDonnell Douglas mainly makes military aircraft.
The US Federal Trade Commission unconditionally cleared the merger on July 1.
